claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment experience rapid degradation during molten-aluminum exposure.
An ultra-thin, well-adhered La2O3 coating will significantly improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
The La2O3 coating will form a stable protective barrier at elevated temperature.
The La2O3 coating will exhibit self-healing behavior upon reaction with molten aluminum.
An ultra-thin La2O3 layer can be applied to the components by a controlled sol-gel or physical-vapor-deposition process.
The intervention should remain effective in molten aluminum at 650–750 degrees Celsius, with typical industrial impurity levels, during extended operationally representative immersion.
The La2O3 layer will physically impede aluminum ingress into the boride substrate.
At the molten-aluminum interface, the La2O3 layer will preferentially react with corrosive species and thereby protect the boride substrate.
La2O3 has sufficient thermodynamic stability and barrier properties at elevated temperature to limit diffusion and chemical attack by molten aluminum.
Dynamic self-healing will continuously repair minor disruptions in the La2O3 barrier during exposure.
Relative to untreated boride components, La2O3-coated samples will show at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate.
The predicted corrosion improvement will be observable through both weight loss and depth-of-attack measurements.
Conventional surface treatments used on these boride components fail to form a robust, adherent barrier against molten aluminum.
Temperatures outside 650–750 degrees Celsius, extreme impurity levels, or mechanical stress may compromise coating integrity.
The long-term adhesion of an ultra-thin La2O3 coating under repeated thermal cycling and mechanical stress has not been fully quantified.
